heading: Polysemantic neurons also arise from initialization, regularization or training noise, not just capacity limits
definition: polysemantic neurons also arise from initialization, regularization or training noise when there are enough neurons for every feature.
summary: Several separate toy-model studies find polysemantic neurons even when there are at least as many neurons as features, each through a different cause: bias initialization and decay, random-initialization collisions under an l1 activation penalty, seed-dependent mixing, or the range of the input sources. Initialization effects appear in several studies, but each regularizer result and the training-noise case rest on a single study, weight decay can instead remove the mixing, and only toy or small networks have been tested.

suggested_status.by_scale: R2 at toy scale only: every V4 test is a toy, synthetic or small biologically inspired network (counts: V4.studies_by_size = {"not stated": 7}; V4.studies_by_stage = {"other": 7}; V4.studies_by_family = {"other or not stated": 7}). No evidence at <1B, 1-10B, 10-100B or >100B.
suggested_status.reason:
No original source is linked (counts: V4.original_sources_linked is empty). Polysemanticity at sufficient capacity in toy networks appears in studies with different titles and years, each through a different mechanism:
- learning rate, bias initialization and weight decay (arXiv:2211.09169, 2022);
- random-initialization collisions under an l1 activation penalty (arXiv:2312.03096, the same experiment as lw:sEyWufriufTnBKnTG);
- seed-dependent residual mixing without weight decay (arXiv:2610.20851, 2026);
- source support (arXiv:2410.06232, ICLR 2025).
The V4 pack headers do not name author groups. The studies index marks one V4 study as SAME GROUP (sharing an author with an original): arXiv:2209.10652, whose V4 verdict is limits_scope, not supports. This matches counts: V4.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 1. The index marks none of the studies listed above (nor lw:sEyWufriufTnBKnTG), so their independence from the original group rests on that author-name match, and their independence from each other is still inferred from titles and years only.
Verdict counts: V4.verdicts.challenges.studies = 0 and V4.verdicts.limits_scope.studies = 3. The limits are a monosemantic n=3, m=6 example (arXiv:2209.10652), weight decay removing mixing (arXiv:2610.20851), and range-independent sources staying modular (arXiv:2410.06232).
Levels by named cause:
- Initialization: seen in several studies with different measures (arXiv:2211.09169, arXiv:2312.03096, arXiv:2610.20851).
- Regularization as a producer: shown with an l1 activation penalty (arXiv:2312.03096#r1, the same experiment as lw:sEyWufriufTnBKnTG#R2), and with weight decay on biases only in arXiv:2211.09169's absolute-value task (k=2048 > N, initial bias -1). There, too high a decay rate gives more polysemantic solutions and slower decay gives more monosemantic ones (arXiv:2211.09169#R12). This decay is part of the negative-bias scheme. The two studies use different regularizers and setups, so neither reproduces the other; each regularizer alone is R0: the index marks neither study as sharing an author with an original, so the bias-only decay result (one study) is R0, and the l1 result is R0 because arXiv:2312.03096 and lw:sEyWufriufTnBKnTG report the same experiment and count as one result whether or not they share authors with each other. The direction depends on the regularizer and setting: weight decay in the exact-capacity encoder removes mixing (arXiv:2610.20851#r7, #r8).
- Training noise: one illustrated instance (arXiv:2312.03096#r2), so R0.
suggested_status.open_questions:
- Would a measurement in a trained vision or language model that separates incidental from capacity-driven polysemantic neurons extend this beyond toy scale?
- Does the Theta(n^2/m) or n^2/(4m) collision count reproduce in a group other than the Incidental authors, and with weight decay or dropout instead of l1?
- Does SGD noise (not injected noise) produce polysemantic neurons, and in what share of runs?
- Would testing an l1 activation penalty, weight decay on all weights and bias-only weight decay in the same setup resolve the regularization disagreement?
- Author check: among the V4 studies, the studies index marks only arXiv:2209.10652 (a limits_scope study, not support) as sharing an author with an original, so no V4 support study carries the mark. The mark compares authors with the originals only, so whether arXiv:2312.03096 and lw:sEyWufriufTnBKnTG share authors with each other is still unchecked. If they do, they are one work reported twice and the l1 result stays R0; only a separate run by a different group would raise it. Neither answer changes the overall level, since they are already treated as one result.
- A failed replication of arXiv:2211.09169's learning-rate and bias-initialization results would move the initialization part toward C.

source.title: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
source.authors: Chris Olah; Nick Cammarata; Ludwig Schubert; Gabriel Goh; Michael Petrov; Shan Carter

original_result.result: The original paper did not test this claim.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: With more neurons than features, learning rate, bias initialization and weight decay decided whether polysemanticity arose.
Polysemantic neurons appeared despite at least one neuron per feature, as chance neuron-sharing at initialization predicts.
A 16-neuron MLP computing Boolean ANDs coded four in one neuron, though neurons outnumbered the ANDs.
Toy autoencoders with enough neurons still formed polysemantic neurons, as chance neuron-sharing at initialization predicts.
Wide toy MLPs still preferred polysemantic zero-loss solutions over basis-aligned ones.
Neurons mixed input sources despite spare neurons when combinations of extreme source values were removed.
Without weight decay, one-neuron-per-feature toy encoders kept polysemantic neurons in some settings and seeds.
With six neurons for three features, the model learned dedicated monosemantic neurons and no polysemantic ones.
Regularized networks with spare neurons kept single-source neurons for sources with independent ranges, even correlated ones.
Weight decay, a regularizer, removed polysemantic neurons here, as did training to convergence.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: Any trained real-world network (image classifier or language model), and how common incidental (non-capacity) polysemantic neurons are in one. Every V4 test uses toy, synthetic or small biologically inspired networks.
untested.basis: counts: V4.studies_by_family = {"other or not stated": 7}; V4.studies_by_size = {"not stated": 7}; V4.studies_by_stage = {"other": 7}. Untested lines of arXiv:2312.03096 (real-world networks and prevalence), lw:sEyWufriufTnBKnTG, arXiv:2610.20851, arXiv:2211.09169 and lw:8EyCQKuWo6swZpagS (real networks). Problems line of arXiv:2410.06232: no prevalence estimate and no canonical AI polysemantic units.

untested.what: Training noise in the sense of SGD or minibatch noise, and any count of polysemantic neurons across runs under noise. The only noise result is one illustrated instance with injected bipolar hidden-layer noise (arXiv:2312.03096#r2).

untested.what: Regularizers other than an l1 activation penalty and weight decay, isolated as a cause; layer norm as a winner-take-all source; co-occurring (non-basis) features in the collision setup. arXiv:2410.06232's networks have L2 penalties on activity and weights, with non-negative activities, but its verdict attributes mixing to source support, not to regularization alone (V4.against[2]).
untested.basis: Untested line of lw:sEyWufriufTnBKnTG (only l1 activation regularization with basis-vector data; other winner-take-all sources and co-occurring features not tested). Untested line of arXiv:2610.20851 (regularization tested only as weight decay). The regularizer of arXiv:2410.06232#R6 (linear RNN, L2 on activity and all weight matrices, non-negative activities; Appendix H.3) is taken from the check on V4.conflicts[1]. Activation nonlinearity is no longer in this item: arXiv:2610.20851 varies the output activation at exact capacity (arXiv:2610.20851#r3 vs #r4, cited in V4.method_sensitivity[5] and V4.wording_issues[1]; V5 rows arXiv:2610.20851#r17 and #r18 compare ReLU, LeakyReLU and linear outputs under weight decay 0.03).

untested.what: Isolating the cause in Boolean-task MLPs and wide one-layer MLPs: initialization, regularization and noise are not separated there, and the local-minima-count hypothesis is not tested.

wording_issues.issue: The direction depends on the regularizer and the setup. An l1 activation penalty goes with polysemantic neurons at m >= n (arXiv:2312.03096#r1, lw:sEyWufriufTnBKnTG#R2). In an exact-capacity encoder (m = n') with a sparse DGP and ReLU output, after 10^6 updates: weight decay 0.01 gives median MCC 0.993 with 9/10 runs >= 0.90, and weight decay 0.03 gives median MCC 0.987 with 10/10 (arXiv:2610.20851#r7, #r8). Removing weight decay lowers MCC to 0.829 +/- 0.029, against 0.994 at 0.03 (#r19). A linear RNN with non-negative activities and an L2 penalty on activity and on all weight matrices (hidden size not stated) stays modular when sources are range-independent (arXiv:2410.06232#R6). In the absolute-value toy model (k=2048 > N=512, initial bias -1), slower weight decay on the biases gives more monosemantic models (arXiv:2211.09169#R12, Figure 23), and Section 4.1.3 says too high a decay rate gives more polysemantic solutions. That decay acts only on biases, within the negative-bias scheme.

wording_issues.phrase: from initialization, regularization or training noise
wording_issues.issue: Other drivers appear at sufficient capacity. Learning rate: in the feature decoder with k=1024 > N=512, low-learning-rate runs are mostly polysemantic at equal loss (arXiv:2211.09169#R1). The data's source support: corner cutting (arXiv:2410.06232#R3, #R4, #R5, #R7). DGP geometry: at exact capacity without weight decay, a hyperspherical DGP retains mixed selectivity with either linear or ReLU output (arXiv:2610.20851#r1, #r2). Output activation: with a sparse DGP and no weight decay, linear output retains mixed selectivity while ReLU output converges slowly to axis alignment (arXiv:2610.20851#r3 vs #r4). The Alignment Forum author hedges: part of the explanation probably involves learning dynamics, the optimizer's (SGD/Adam) inductive biases and initialization (lw:8EyCQKuWo6swZpagS#R2, footnote 13).

The only test is injected bipolar hidden-layer noise (sigma = 0.01) in one illustrated autoencoder instance, with n and m not stated (arXiv:2312.03096#r2). SGD noise is not tested (arXiv:2610.20851 untested line). The phrase could mean either.

wording_issues.phrase: when there are enough neurons for every feature
wording_issues.issue: Tested capacity ranges from exact (m = n', arXiv:2610.20851) up to k=2048 neurons for N=512 features. arXiv:2211.09169 uses k=1024 in its learning-rate runs (#R1), sweeps width from k=16 to 2048 (Figures 15-17, #R4), and uses k=2048 in its absolute-value runs. Other ranges: m from 256 to 4096 for n=256 (arXiv:2312.03096#r1), and 25 hidden units for 2 sources (arXiv:2410.06232#R3). Width is varied in arXiv:2312.03096 and arXiv:2211.09169. In arXiv:2312.03096 the polysemantic count falls with m as Theta(n^2/m) (#r1). In arXiv:2211.09169, extra neurons above k=N mostly add monosemantic neurons, and no polysemantic-neuron count against width is reported (#R4). At n=3, m=6, Toy Models reports no polysemanticity (arXiv:2209.10652, text). In the feature decoder, the residual polysemantic count tracks embedding dimension d, measured by a bias proxy: 65 positive-bias neurons at d=64, and 33 and 130 neurons with bias > 0.05 at d=32 and d=128 (arXiv:2211.09169#R7, #R8, #R9).

The studies measure different constructs: a positive-bias or bias > 0.05 proxy (arXiv:2211.09169#R7, #R8, #R9); MCC axis alignment of latents (arXiv:2610.20851#r1 to #r8); conditional-information modularity or mixed selectivity (arXiv:2410.06232#R4, #R5); weight inspection of single neurons (arXiv:2504.08842#r1); and polysemantic-neuron counts (arXiv:2312.03096#r1). None measures neurons in a trained vision or language model (counts: V4.studies_by_family = {"other or not stated": 7}).

method_sensitivity.what: In the exact-capacity sparse-ReLU encoder at 10^6 updates: weight decay 0 gives median MCC 0.878 with 3/10 runs >= 0.90 (r5); 0.003 gives 0.946 with 7/10 (r6); 0.01 gives 0.993 with 9/10 (r7); 0.03 gives 0.987 with 10/10 (r8). Removing weight decay gives 0.829 +/- 0.029 against 0.994 at 0.03 (r19). The spread across seeds at weight decay 0 is the initialization dependence. In the absolute-value toy model, polysemantic outcomes depend on the weight-decay rate (arXiv:2211.09169#R12).

In the feature decoder (N=512, k=1024), runs at different learning rates reach indistinguishable loss, but low-learning-rate runs are mostly polysemantic (R1). At learning rate 0.03 and zero initial mean bias, 503/512 features had one monosemantic neuron (R3).

In the feature decoder, a negative initial mean bias (about -1) gives highly monosemantic solutions (R2; weight decay was off for the final 50% of training). In the absolute-value model, a negative initial bias alone did not reliably suffice, and outcomes depended on weight decay (R12).

The number of polysemantic neurons follows a Theta(n^2/m) trend in hidden width m for n=256, m from 256 to 4096 (arXiv:2312.03096#r1, lw:sEyWufriufTnBKnTG#R2). In highly monosemantic feature decoders, the residual polysemantic count tracks embedding dimension d: 33 at d=32, 65 at d=64, 130 at d=128 (arXiv:2211.09169#R8, #R7, #R9).

method_sensitivity.factor: Data distribution: source support and DGP geometry
method_sensitivity.what: Corner-cut (range-dependent) source support produces mixed units in surplus-capacity networks (arXiv:2410.06232#R3, #R4, #R5, #R7). Range-independent sources, including correlated ones, stay modular (#R6). At exact capacity, a hyperspherical DGP retains mixed selectivity (arXiv:2610.20851#r1, #r2), while a sparse DGP with ReLU output converges to axis-aligned neurons (#r4).

With a sparse non-negative exponential DGP at exact capacity, a linear output retains mixed selectivity (r3, figure only) and a non-negative ReLU output converges to axis-aligned neurons (r4, figure only).

method_sensitivity.factor: Which sources the selectivity analysis conditions on
method_sensitivity.what: The method-sensitivity line of arXiv:2410.06232 says apparent selectivity changes depending on whether the analysis conditions on all encoded sources or leaves one out. No V4 row records numbers for this.

status_amendment.public_note: A check of author names now shows that one study on this claim, Toy Models of Superposition, shares authors with the original papers; that study only limits the claim, and the check flags none of the supporting toy-model studies, though it would not catch authors who share only an affiliation. The suggested level stays R2 and still covers toy models only.
